subject: PHS
subtopic: Communicating with patients with disabilities and interpreters
vignette: A 32-year-old man who uses a wheelchair presents to his primary care physician with 2 days of painful, draining right ear pain and decreased hearing. A medical student taking the history opens by asking detailed questions about how long he has used the wheelchair and whether his mobility is declining.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate modification to the student's approach?

options.text: Continue exploring the wheelchair use, because mobility status is always pertinent to the chief complaint.
Refocus the interview on the ear symptoms, since the disability should not be brought up when it is not relevant to the visit.
Proceed with the history but omit the ear examination, because examining a patient seated in a wheelchair is too challenging.
Direct further questions to the accompanying family member instead of the patient.
Explain to the patient that people with his condition frequently develop ear infections.

explanation_correct: First Aid guidance is that, as with any other part of the medical history, a disability should not be brought up if it is not relevant to the visit — a patient in a wheelchair with an ear infection is the exact example given. The interview and examination should center on the presenting complaint. Relevance to the chief complaint, not the presence of a disability, determines what is asked.

explanation_incorrect.A: Although mobility history is sometimes relevant, in this vignette the ear infection is the reason for the visit, and the disability is not pertinent to it. Probing it adds no diagnostic value and risks making the patient feel defined by his disability.
explanation_incorrect.C: Relevant parts of the physical examination should never be skipped even if the disability makes the examination more challenging; the clinician should adapt how the examination is performed rather than omit it.
explanation_incorrect.D: Under most circumstances the physician should talk directly to the patient. Accompanying caregivers can add information as needed, but they should not replace the patient as the primary source.
explanation_incorrect.E: This statement is falsely reassuring and stereotypes the patient on the basis of his disability. It offers no useful medical information and is not an appropriate way to open the encounter.

educationalObjective: Do not raise a patient's disability during a visit unless it is relevant to the presenting problem, and never skip relevant examination parts because a disability makes them challenging.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Communicating with patients with disabilities and interpreters
vignette: A 44-year-old woman who is deaf arrives for a new-patient visit accompanied by her teenage son, who offers to interpret. She has never been seen at this clinic before, and the intake form contains no information about how she prefers to communicate.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?

options.text: Use her son as the interpreter, since he is present and readily available.
Begin writing all questions and instructions on paper without further discussion.
Remove her face covering, face the patient, and speak at a normal volume so she can lipread.
Ask the patient what her preferred mode of communication is before starting the interview.
Speak loudly and slowly to ensure the patient understands the questions.

explanation_correct: Patients who are deaf or hard of hearing should be asked their preferred mode of communication rather than having one assumed for them. Some patients prefer sign language interpretation, some prefer to speak and lipread, and others prefer writing; only the patient can say which works best. This preference question should come before the substantive interview begins.

explanation_incorrect.A: While a patient may prefer a family member, that preference should be elicited and recorded in the chart — not assumed because a relative happens to be present. For deaf patients specifically, the first step is asking the preferred mode of communication.
explanation_incorrect.B: Writing may be one patient's preferred mode, but imposing it without asking substitutes the physician's assumption for the patient's stated preference and can miss patients who prefer interpretation or lipreading.
explanation_incorrect.C: Facing the patient and keeping speech at a normal mode is appropriate for patients who have already chosen to speak and lipread. It should not be assumed before the patient is asked what she prefers.
explanation_incorrect.E: Speaking loudly and slowly does not help most deaf patients and changing one's mode of speaking is specifically discouraged for those who lipread. Deafness is not resolved by increased volume.

educationalObjective: For patients who are deaf or hard of hearing, always ask their preferred mode of communication first; do not assume sign, lipreading, writing, or family interpretation.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Communicating with patients with disabilities and interpreters
vignette: A 67-year-old woman with limited English proficiency presents to the emergency department with chest tightness. The triage nurse notes that her daughter, who is fluent in English, is in the waiting room, and a bilingual hospital volunteer is available on the unit. The physician does not speak the patient's language.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to proceed with this encounter?

options.text: Use a professionally trained medical interpreter, arranging telephone or video interpretation if no in-person interpreter is available.
Proceed in English, because the patient has nodded appropriately to the triage questions.
Have the daughter interpret, and document her role as the preferred interpreter in the chart.
Ask the bilingual volunteer to translate the history, since a trained interpreter is not immediately present.
Defer the full interview until an in-person interpreter becomes available, and obtain no history in the interim.

explanation_correct: Visits with a patient who speaks little English should use a professionally trained medical interpreter unless the physician is conversationally fluent in the patient's preferred language. If an in-person interpreter is unavailable, interpretation by telephone or video call is an acceptable substitute, so the interview need not be deferred. This patient's chest pain history is too important to route through untrained staff or family.

explanation_incorrect.B: Nodding does not demonstrate conversational fluency or comprehension of medical questions. Assuming adequate English and proceeding without an interpreter risks a critically inaccurate history in a patient with possible cardiac disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: A family member's preference should only be honored if the patient herself prefers it and it is recorded in the chart; even then, a professionally trained interpreter is the standard unless the physician is conversationally fluent. The patient's preference has not been elicited here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bilingual volunteers are not professionally trained medical interpreters and may lack the medical vocabulary and interpretation technique needed for an accurate, complete history in a chest-pain evaluation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Deferring the interview entirely is unnecessary: interpretation services may be provided by telephone or video call when no in-person interpreter is available, so a proper history can be obtained promptly.

educationalObjective: Use a professionally trained medical interpreter for patients with limited English proficiency (in person or by telephone/video) unless the physician is conversationally fluent in the patient's language.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Communicating with patients with disabilities and interpreters
vignette: A physician is evaluating a 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes using a professionally trained, in-person Spanish interpreter for the first time. The physician speaks no Spanish, and this is a routine outpatient visit without time pressure.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate technique for conducting this interview?

options.text: Address the interpreter with commands such as "Ask him what he eats in the morning" to keep the exchange efficient.
Ask the patient several questions at once so the interpreter can translate them in a single block.
Position the interpreter next to the physician so that the patient's attention is directed toward the interpreter.
Speak directly to the interpreter and maintain eye contact with the interpreter throughout the interview.
Make eye contact with the patient, speak directly to him, and ask one question at a time.

explanation_correct: When working with an interpreter, the physician should make eye contact with the patient and speak to them directly, avoiding third-person statements such as "tell him." Extra time should be allowed for the interview, and questions should be posed one at a time. These techniques keep the patient — not the interpreter — at the center of the encounter.

explanation_incorrect.A: Third-person statements directed at the interpreter, such as "tell him," are specifically discouraged. Questions should be spoken directly to the patient in the first person.
explanation_incorrect.B: Multiple questions asked at once confuse interpretation and the patient's responses. The guideline is to ask one question at a time and allow extra time for the interview.
explanation_incorrect.C: For in-person spoken-language interpretation, the interpreter should ideally be positioned next to or slightly behind the patient, not next to the physician. (Beside the physician is the recommended position for sign language interpreters.)
explanation_incorrect.D: Eye contact should be directed at the patient, not the interpreter. Speaking to the interpreter rather than the patient depersonalizes the encounter and contradicts direct-communication guidance.

educationalObjective: With an interpreter, speak directly to the patient in the first person, maintain eye contact with the patient, ask one question at a time, and allow extra time.
